entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To reach an agreement or produce a detailed plan through long, hard discussion and negotiation.
entries.usage: Common in news and business talk about deals, contracts, budgets and treaties: *hammer out a deal, an agreement, the details*. It stresses the effort and the arguing it took. A noun object usually comes after *out*, and a pronoun goes in the middle: *hammer it out*.
entries.pattern: hammer out a deal / an agreement / a compromise
examples: After weeks of talks, the two airlines **hammered out** an agreement to share routes across the Atlantic.
My ex and I finally **hammered out** a custody schedule that works for both of us.
Our condo board spent months **hammering out** new rules for short-term rentals.

drill.sentence: The city and the teachers' union {{hammered out}} a deal at three in the morning, so schools will open on Monday after all.
drill.hint: produced after long, tough bargaining (not *worked out* or *struck*)

entries.related: *iron out* — settle the last small problems in a deal; *work out* — more general and neutral; *thrash out* — similar, more British.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To deal with a problem, mistake or unpleasant fact only very briefly, or skip it, so that people don't pay attention to it.
entries.usage: Usually critical: people accuse a report, speech or apology of *glossing over* the problems, risks or details. It is inseparable, so the object follows *over*: *gloss over it*. It is often used with *quickly* or in the passive: *The issue was glossed over.*
entries.pattern: gloss over the problems / risks / details
examples: The CEO's letter **glossed over** the layoffs and focused on record profits.
My dad always **glosses over** the part of the story where he got lost.
History textbooks often **gloss over** the uglier parts of a country's past.

drill.sentence: The doctor {{glossed over}} the side effects, so I only found out about them from the pharmacist.
drill.hint: dealt with too quickly, as if they didn't matter (not *skipped* or *skimmed over*)

entries.related: *skate over* — very similar; *sweep under the rug* — hide a problem completely; *play down* — make something seem less serious than it is.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To make something seem less important, serious or impressive than it really is.
entries.usage: Common in news about officials and companies (*play down fears, the risks, reports of …*) and about modest people (*She plays down her role*). A noun object can go before or after *down*; a pronoun goes in the middle: *play it down*. The one-word verb *downplay* means the same and is very common in American writing.
entries.pattern: play down the risks / fears / reports; play it down
examples: Officials tried to **play down** the risk, but people still lined up to buy bottled water.
He's been **playing down** his knee injury, but he's clearly limping.
My grandfather always **played down** what he did in the war; we only learned the details after he died.

drill.sentence: When my mom asked about the fender bender, I {{played it down}} so she wouldn't worry.
drill.hint: made it seem less serious (not *downplayed* or *made light of*)

entries.related: *downplay* — same meaning, one word; *gloss over* — mention a problem only briefly; *play up* — the opposite.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To emphasize a quality or fact so that it seems more important or impressive than it might otherwise.
entries.usage: Common in ads, campaigns, job applications and news coverage: *play up the benefits, her experience, the rivalry*. It suggests a deliberate choice of what to highlight, sometimes a slightly misleading one. A pronoun goes in the middle (*play it up*); note that British *play up* also means misbehave, a sense Americans rarely use.
entries.pattern: play up the benefits / a connection / your experience
examples: The ad **plays up** the car's safety features and barely mentions the price.
In your cover letter, **play up** the leadership experience from your volunteer work.
Sports networks love to **play up** the rivalry between the two quarterbacks.

drill.sentence: To get her parents to say yes to the trip, Maya {{played up}} the educational side and didn't mention the beach parties.
drill.hint: made it sound bigger and more important (not *talked up*)

entries.related: *talk up* — praise something in speech to make it sound good; *highlight* — neutral, no hint of exaggeration; *play down* — the opposite.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To speak about something with great enthusiasm so that it sounds better or more attractive than it may really be.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and news about products, places, candidates, events and plans: people *talk up* a restaurant, a stock, a teammate, the economy. It often hints that the praise is exaggerated or self-interested. A noun object can go before or after *up*; a pronoun goes in the middle: *talk it up*.
entries.pattern: talk up a product / plan / person; talk it up
examples: My brother had been **talking up** this taco place for weeks, and honestly, it was just okay.
The real estate agent spent the whole tour **talking up** the neighborhood's new parks and restaurants.
Investors who **talk up** a stock on social media sometimes sell it quietly the next day.

drill.sentence: My friends had {{talked up}} the movie so much that I was a little disappointed when I finally saw it.
drill.hint: praised enthusiastically when chatting (not *hyped* or *built up*)

entries.related: *hype (up)* — promote very strongly, often in the media; *play up* — emphasize one feature; *rave about* — praise with great excitement; *talk down* — criticize to make something seem less valuable.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To try to express or suggest something, especially indirectly or without saying it clearly.
entries.usage: Almost always in the progressive, in questions and *what* clauses: *What are you getting at?*, *That's what I was getting at.* Said sharply, *What are you getting at?* suggests you suspect a hidden criticism, while *I see what you're getting at* is friendly. It is inseparable, and *at* usually ends the clause.
entries.pattern: What are you getting at?; what I'm getting at is …
examples: You keep mentioning how late I got home last night. What are you **getting at**?
I think I see what the author is **getting at**, but the essay never says it outright.
What I'm **getting at** is that we can't afford a new car and a vacation this year.

drill.sentence: Mom, you've asked me three times if I'm eating enough. What exactly are you {{getting at}}?
drill.hint: trying to say indirectly (not *implying*, *hinting at* or *driving at*)

entries.related: *drive at* — same meaning, a bit old-fashioned; *imply* — more formal; *hint at* — suggest something gently; *get at someone* — British, criticize someone repeatedly.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To start discussing or explaining a subject in detail.
entries.usage: Very common in speech, often in the negative to avoid a topic: *Let's not get into that now*, *I don't want to get into it.* In talks and meetings, *Before we get into the details …* signals the start of a detailed part. It is inseparable: *get into the details*, never *get the details into*.
entries.pattern: let's not get into it; get into the details / politics
examples: It's a long story, and I'd rather not **get into** it right now.
Before we **get into** the numbers, let me give you some background.
The article never really **gets into** why rents rose so fast in the first place.

drill.sentence: My brother and I had a huge fight over Thanksgiving, but I really don't want to {{get into}} it.
drill.hint: start discussing it in detail (not *go into* or *talk about*)

entries.related: *go into* — explain in detail, slightly more formal; *get into it (with someone)* — also means start arguing; *touch on* — mention briefly.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To continue for much longer than necessary or wanted, in a slow and tiring way.
entries.usage: Used for meetings, wars, lawsuits, negotiations, illnesses and winters, always with a sense of frustration. It is intransitive: the event itself *drags on*, often *for months* or *and on*. The transitive form is *drag something out*: make it last longer than needed.
entries.pattern: the meeting / war / case drags on (for months)
examples: The meeting **dragged on** for three hours, and we still didn't make a decision.
The divorce **dragged on** for two years and cost them a fortune in legal fees.
As the war **drags on**, more and more families are leaving the region.

drill.sentence: Winter always seems to {{drag on}} in Chicago; it's still snowing in April.
drill.hint: last much longer than you want (not just *go on*)

entries.related: *drag something out* — make something last longer than needed; *go on and on* — continue in a boring way; *wrap up* — the opposite, finish.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To think carefully about an idea, offer or decision for some time before deciding.
entries.usage: Common when you need time before answering: *Let me mull it over*, *I'm still mulling it over.* It sounds calm and thoughtful, and it is a polite way to delay a decision. A noun object can go before or after *over*; a pronoun goes in the middle: *mull it over*.
entries.pattern: mull over an offer / idea; mull it over
examples: She's **mulling over** a job offer in Seattle, but she doesn't want to leave her parents.
Thanks for the proposal. Let me **mull it over** this weekend, and I'll get back to you Monday.
We're still **mulling over** whether to sell the house or rent it out.

drill.sentence: It's a big decision, so take a few days to {{mull it over}} before you sign the lease.
drill.hint: consider it slowly and carefully (not *think it over* or *sleep on it*)

entries.related: *think something over* — same, more common and neutral; *chew on* — informal, think about for a while; *sleep on it* — wait until tomorrow to decide.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To direct all your attention to one particular thing, person or problem, often after narrowing down the options.
entries.usage: Used in neutral speech and writing about searches, investigations and problem solving: doctors, police and buyers *zero in on* a cause, a suspect or a house. It suggests narrowing the focus step by step, like aiming at a target. It is inseparable: *zero in on the problem*.
entries.pattern: zero in on a cause / suspect / problem
examples: After weeks of tests, the doctors finally **zeroed in on** the cause of her headaches.
Investigators quickly **zeroed in on** a former employee who still had a key.
The interviewer **zeroed in on** the one weak spot in my application.

drill.sentence: After reading dozens of reviews, I {{zeroed in on}} one laptop that had everything I needed.
drill.hint: narrowed my focus to, like aiming at a target (not *honed in on* or *settled on*)

entries.related: *home in on* — very similar, more common in British English; *hone in on* — a common American variant that many editors call an error; *focus on* — neutral; *narrow down* — reduce a list of options.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To rely confidently on something happening, or on someone doing something, especially when you make plans.
entries.usage: Informal and common in speech; *I wouldn't bank on it* is a standard way to say something is unlikely. It is inseparable, and the object can be a noun, an *-ing* form or *someone doing something*: *Don't bank on him showing up.*
entries.pattern: bank on + noun / -ing / someone doing something; I wouldn't bank on it
examples: We're **banking on** good weather, because the wedding is outdoors and there's no tent.
The ski resort is **banking on** a snowy winter after two bad seasons.
He might pay you back by Friday, but I wouldn't **bank on** it.

drill.sentence: Don't {{bank on}} getting a tax refund this year; plan your budget as if you won't.
drill.hint: treat as certain when you plan (not *count on*)

entries.related: *count on* — same, more neutral and also used for people (*count on me*); *rely on* — more formal; *gamble on* — take a risk on something uncertain.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To depend completely on one thing, so that the outcome changes if that thing changes.
entries.usage: More formal than *depend on*, typical of news, law, analysis and serious discussion: *The case hinges on one witness.* The subject is an outcome, decision or argument, and the object is often a *whether* clause. It is inseparable; *hinge upon* is a more formal variant.
entries.pattern: X hinges on Y / on whether …
examples: The whole case **hinges on** the testimony of a single witness.
Our vacation plans **hinge on** whether my husband can get the week off.
The team's playoff hopes **hinge on** Sunday's game against Dallas.

drill.sentence: Whether the outdoor concert goes ahead {{hinges on}} the weather forecast for Saturday.
drill.hint: is entirely decided by (not *depends on*, *rests on* or *comes down to*)

entries.related: *depend on* — neutral and general; *turn on* — very similar, formal; *come down to* — what decides the result in the end; *rest on* — be based on.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To control or limit something more strictly, such as spending, a person's behavior or a strong feeling.
entries.usage: Common in news, business and everyday talk: *rein in spending, costs, inflation*, or *rein in* a powerful agency or a hot-tempered player. It suggests something had become too free and now needs control again. A noun object usually follows *in*, and a pronoun goes in the middle: *rein it in*.
entries.pattern: rein in spending / costs / inflation; rein it in
examples: After the holidays, we really need to **rein in** our spending on takeout.
The new law is meant to **rein in** the power of the largest tech companies.
The coach told him to **rein in** his temper or he'd be benched.

drill.sentence: The central bank raised interest rates again to {{rein in}} inflation.
drill.hint: get under control, like a rider with a horse (not *bring down*)

mistake.wrong: The city needs to reign in its spending.
mistake.right: The city needs to rein in its spending.
mistake.why: The image is a rider pulling a horse's *reins*; *reign* is what a king does.

entries.related: *curb* — limit, more formal; *crack down on* — take strong action against bad behavior; *let loose* — the opposite, free from control.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To become gradually smaller, weaker or less frequent until it stops completely.
entries.usage: Used for trails, roads, conversations, interest, support and rain. It describes a quiet, slow ending rather than a sudden one, and it often sounds slightly disappointed. It is intransitive: the thing itself *peters out*, often with *gradually* or *eventually*.
entries.pattern: the trail / conversation / interest petered out
examples: Our book club met every month for a year, and then it just **petered out**.
Donations **petered out** after the news coverage moved on to other stories.
The rain **petered out** around noon, so we went for a walk after lunch.

drill.sentence: The trail {{petered out}} near the creek, and we had to find our own way back to the car.
drill.hint: gradually got fainter and then stopped (not just *ended*)

entries.related: *fizzle out* — end weakly after a promising start; *taper off* — decrease gradually, often as planned; *die down* — become quieter or less intense.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To end weakly or disappointingly, after a start that seemed exciting or promising.
entries.usage: Informal and common for protests, campaigns, romances, storms and comebacks in sports. Unlike *peter out*, it stresses the gap between a strong start and a weak ending. It is intransitive, and *fizzle* alone is also used: *The plan fizzled.*
entries.pattern: the protest / romance / rally fizzled out
examples: The protests drew huge crowds at first, but they **fizzled out** within a month.
Their summer romance **fizzled out** as soon as school started again.
The Mets' late rally **fizzled out** with a strikeout in the ninth inning.

drill.sentence: My New Year's resolution to run every morning {{fizzled out}} by mid-January.
drill.hint: ended weakly after an enthusiastic start (not *petered out*)

entries.related: *peter out* — fade slowly, with less focus on the strong start; *fall flat* — fail to impress at all; *go nowhere* — make no progress.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To decrease gradually in amount, number or intensity.
entries.usage: Neutral and common for rain, sales, symptoms, traffic and growth: *Sales tapered off after the holidays.* It describes a smooth, steady decline, not a sudden drop. It is mostly intransitive, but in medicine you can also *taper off* a drug, meaning reduce the dose step by step.
entries.pattern: sales / rain / symptoms taper off; taper off a medication
examples: The rain should **taper off** by this evening, so the game will probably go ahead.
Sales of the new phone were strong at first but **tapered off** after a few months.
My doctor wants me to **taper off** the steroids slowly instead of stopping all at once.

drill.sentence: Traffic usually {{tapers off}} after seven, so let's leave a little later.
drill.hint: gets gradually lighter (not *dies down*, *lets up* or *thins out*)

entries.related: *peter out* — fade until it stops completely; *drop off* — decrease, often suddenly; *level off* — stop rising or falling and stay the same.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To persuade someone to do something, often something they didn't want to do at first.
entries.usage: Very common in everyday speech: *She talked me into it.* The person always goes between *talk* and *into*, and *into* is followed by a noun or an *-ing* form, never *to* + verb. The opposite is *talk someone out of something*.
entries.pattern: talk someone into + noun / -ing
examples: My sister **talked me into** running a half marathon with her, and now I'm hooked.
The salesman **talked us into** the extended warranty, which we never used.
She **talked her boss into** letting the whole team work from home on Fridays.

drill.sentence: I wasn't planning to adopt a dog, but my kids {{talked me into}} it.
drill.hint: persuaded me by speaking (not *pushed* or *pressured*)

mistake.wrong: My friend talked me to join the gym.
mistake.right: My friend talked me into joining the gym.
mistake.why: *Talk someone into* takes a noun or an *-ing* form, unlike *persuade someone to do*.

entries.related: *persuade / convince someone to do something* — more formal; *talk someone out of something* — persuade them not to; *pressure someone into* — push them hard.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To persuade someone who was doubtful or opposed to support you, agree with you or like you.
entries.usage: Common for voters, in-laws, skeptical colleagues, audiences and customers. It implies they were not on your side at first, and the means often follows *with*: *She won us over with her honesty.* A pronoun goes in the middle (*win them over*), while a longer noun object can follow *over*: *win over undecided voters*.
entries.pattern: win someone over (with something); win over voters / critics
examples: My dad didn't like my boyfriend at first, but Jake **won him over** by helping fix the fence.
Opening night was rough, but by the end of the run the cast had **won over** even the toughest critics.
I was skeptical about the new bakery, but the croissants **won me over**.

drill.sentence: The kids thought their new teacher was too strict, but she quickly {{won them over}} with her silly jokes.
drill.hint: got them on her side (not *charmed them*)

entries.related: *bring someone around* — persuade them to change their opinion; *charm* — win someone's liking through personality; *alienate* — the opposite, make people turn against you.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To tell someone an idea or plan in order to get their quick reaction or opinion.
entries.usage: Informal and very common at work and among friends: *Can I bounce something off you?* The idea goes between *bounce* and *off*, and the person comes after *off*. It suggests a casual, quick check, not a formal review.
entries.pattern: bounce an idea / something off someone
examples: Do you have a minute? I'd like to **bounce** a few ideas **off** you before the pitch.
Before I quit, I **bounced** the plan **off** my older sister, who's been freelancing for years.
The writers in our group **bounce** story ideas **off** each other every Thursday night.

drill.sentence: I have an idea for Mom's birthday party. Can I {{bounce it off}} you before I tell the others?
drill.hint: share it quickly to hear what you think (not *run it by*)

entries.related: *run something by someone* — very similar, often to get approval; *sound someone out* — find out someone's opinion carefully; *brainstorm* — produce ideas as a group.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To interrupt a conversation or get involved in something rudely, when nobody asked you to.
entries.usage: Informal and critical: it describes joining uninvited, as in *Nobody asked you to butt in.* People also say *Sorry to butt in, but …* to make their own interruption sound polite. It is intransitive; use *butt in on* a conversation or *butt into* someone's business.
entries.pattern: butt in (on a conversation); Sorry to butt in, but …
examples: We were having a private conversation when my coworker **butted in** with his opinion.
Sorry to **butt in**, but I couldn't help overhearing that you're from Ohio too.
My mother-in-law keeps **butting in** whenever we make a decision about the kids.

drill.sentence: My little brother always {{butts in}} whenever I'm on the phone with my girlfriend.
drill.hint: rudely interrupts (not *cuts in* or *barges in*)

entries.related: *cut in* — interrupt, less rude; *chime in* — join a conversation in a friendly way; *butt out* — (rude) stop interfering; *barge in* — enter a room or conversation rudely.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To say something suddenly and without thinking, often something you should have kept private.
entries.usage: Used for secrets, answers, confessions and awkward remarks, often with a sense of embarrassment. A noun object can go before or after *out*, and a pronoun goes in the middle: *blurt it out*. *Blurt* alone is also common with direct speech: *'I'm pregnant,' she blurted.*
entries.pattern: blurt out a secret / the answer; blurt it out
examples: I was so nervous that I **blurted out** the answer before he finished the question.
My nephew **blurted out** that we'd bought her a puppy, so the surprise was ruined.
In a live interview, the actor **blurted out** the ending of his new movie before it opened.

drill.sentence: I promised not to tell anyone about the engagement, but I {{blurted it out}} at dinner.
drill.hint: said it suddenly without thinking (not *let it slip*)

entries.related: *let something slip* — reveal by accident; *spill the beans* — reveal a secret, informal; *come out with* — say something surprising.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To keep talking about the same subject, especially a complaint or someone's mistake, in a way that annoys people.
entries.usage: Informal and critical, often with *keep* or *always*: *She keeps harping on my grades.* Americans say *harp on* + the topic, while British speakers also say *harp on about*. It is inseparable, and *Stop harping on it* is a common complaint.
entries.pattern: keep harping on + noun
examples: My dad still **harps on** the time I crashed his car, and that was ten years ago.
My dentist keeps **harping on** flossing, even though I've gotten much better about it.
I know the report was late. You don't need to keep **harping on** it.

drill.sentence: Okay, I forgot your birthday last year, but do you have to keep {{harping on}} it?
drill.hint: talking about it again and again in an annoying way (not *dwelling on* or *going on about*)

entries.related: *go on about* — talk too long about something; *dwell on* — keep thinking about something negative; *nag* — keep asking someone to do something.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To speak to someone as if they were less intelligent or less important than you.
entries.usage: Always critical: it describes a condescending tone, a typical complaint about doctors, managers, salespeople and experts. It is inseparable, and the person always comes after *to*. *Patronize* and *condescend to* mean the same and sound more formal.
entries.pattern: talk down to someone
examples: I hate it when car mechanics **talk down to** me just because I'm a woman.
Good teachers explain hard ideas simply without **talking down to** their students.
The best children's books never **talk down to** their readers.

drill.sentence: The guy at the phone store explained what Wi-Fi was, as if I were five. He was really {{talking down to}} me.
drill.hint: treating me as stupid when speaking (not *patronizing* or *condescending to*)

entries.related: *patronize* — same meaning, also about actions; *condescend to* — more formal; *talk someone down* — calm someone, or get a seller to lower a price.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To keep thinking or talking about something unpleasant or sad for longer than is useful.
entries.usage: Usually in advice and in the negative: *Don't dwell on it*, *There's no point dwelling on the past.* Typical objects are mistakes, the past, failures, bad news and regrets. It is inseparable; *dwell upon* is a more formal variant.
entries.pattern: dwell on the past / mistakes / what went wrong
examples: Everyone makes mistakes at work, so try not to **dwell on** this one.
After the breakup, she spent months **dwelling on** what she could have done differently.
The coach told reporters the team wouldn't **dwell on** last week's loss.

drill.sentence: Yes, the trip was a disaster, but there's no point {{dwelling on}} it now; let's plan the next one.
drill.hint: continuing to think about something negative (not *obsessing over*)

entries.related: *brood over* — think unhappily about something for a long time; *harp on* — keep talking about it annoyingly; *move on* — the opposite, stop thinking about it.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To go over something quickly from start to finish, to check it, explain it or practice it.
entries.usage: Common before presentations, performances and trips: *Let's run through the plan, your lines, the checklist.* It is inseparable: *run through it*, not *run it through* in this sense. The noun *run-through* means a practice performance or a quick review.
entries.pattern: run through the plan / slides / your lines
examples: Let's **run through** the slides one more time before the client gets here.
Before we leave, I'll **run through** the checklist: passports, chargers, snacks.
The actors **ran through** the final scene twice before the doors opened.

drill.sentence: The night before the wedding, the best man {{ran through}} his speech in front of the mirror.
drill.hint: practiced from start to finish (not *went over* or *rehearsed*)

entries.related: *go over* — review or check carefully; *rehearse* — practice a performance, more formal; *skim* — read quickly without detail.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To divide something complex, such as a cost, task or set of results, into smaller parts so that it is easier to understand or analyze.
entries.usage: Very common in explanations, budgets and statistics: *break down the costs*, *break it down for me*, *broken down by age*. A noun object can go before or after *down*; a pronoun goes in the middle. The noun *breakdown* is the result: *a breakdown of the costs*.
entries.pattern: break down the costs / numbers (by age); break it down for someone
examples: Can you **break down** the bill so I know what each of us owes?
The survey results are **broken down** by age and income.
A good coach **breaks** a complicated move **down** into small, simple steps.

drill.sentence: The contractor's quote was just one big number, so I asked him to {{break it down}} for me.
drill.hint: split it into separate parts (not *itemize it*)

entries.related: *itemize* — list costs one by one; *unpack* — explain the ideas inside something; *spell out* — explain clearly and fully.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To explain or present a plan, argument or set of facts clearly and in an organized way.
entries.usage: Common in meetings, speeches, reports and journalism: *lay out a plan, a case, the options, a vision*. It suggests a clear, step-by-step presentation. A noun object usually follows *out*, and a pronoun goes in the middle: *Let me lay it out for you.*
entries.pattern: lay out a plan / the options / a case
examples: In her first meeting with the staff, the new CEO **laid out** her plan to turn the company around.
Our financial adviser **laid out** three options for paying off our student loans.
Let me **lay it out** for you: if we don't fix the roof now, it'll cost twice as much next year.

drill.sentence: Before we pick a college, let's sit down and {{lay out}} all the options with their costs.
drill.hint: present clearly and in order (not *go over* or *set out*)

entries.related: *set out* — similar, more formal and more British; *spell out* — explain in full detail, often impatiently; *outline* — describe the main points.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To start an activity with a clear plan or intention to achieve a particular result.
entries.usage: Common in stories, biographies, reviews and mission statements: *She set out to prove them wrong.* It often compares the original aim with the result: *what we set out to do*, *I never set out to …*. It is followed by *to* + verb; *set out* on its own often means start a journey.
entries.pattern: set out to + verb; what we set out to do
examples: She **set out to** prove that a small bakery could compete with the big chains.
I never **set out to** become a teacher; it just kind of happened.
The documentary **sets out to** explain why housing costs so much in California.

drill.sentence: We {{set out to}} hike the whole trail in a week, but my knee gave out after three days.
drill.hint: began with the clear intention to (not *planned to* or *aimed to*)

entries.related: *aim to* — have as a goal, more neutral; *set about* — start doing a task; *set out* (without *to*) — start a journey.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To investigate or examine something thoroughly in order to find out more about it.
entries.usage: Informal but common at work and in journalism: *dig into the numbers, the records, someone's past*. It suggests effort and curiosity, like digging below the surface. It is inseparable, and it can also mean start eating hungrily: *We dug into the pasta.*
entries.pattern: dig into the records / numbers / someone's past
examples: Reporters started **digging into** the charity's finances after the story broke.
When we **dug into** the logs, we found the crashes started after Tuesday's update.
I've been **digging into** my family history and found relatives in Norway.

drill.sentence: Before buying the used car, I {{dug into}} its accident history online.
drill.hint: investigated thoroughly (not *looked into*)

entries.related: *look into* — investigate, more neutral and less thorough; *delve into* — more formal; *dig up* — find hidden facts, often damaging ones.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To read a lot about a subject in order to learn about it, often to prepare for something.
entries.usage: Common when preparing for a trip, an interview, a diagnosis or a decision: *I need to read up on it.* It is inseparable and takes *on* (less often *about*) before the topic. In the past tense, *read up* is pronounced like *red up*.
entries.pattern: read up on + topic
examples: Before our trip to Japan, I **read up on** local customs so I wouldn't offend anyone.
After my dad's diagnosis, I **read up on** everything about type 2 diabetes.
Make sure you **read up on** the company before the interview.

drill.sentence: My son is obsessed with sharks, and I've been {{reading up on}} them just to answer all his questions.
drill.hint: studying through books and articles (not *researching* or *looking into*)

entries.related: *brush up on* — improve knowledge or skills you already had; *look into* — investigate; *bone up on* — study hard, informal.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To speak openly and honestly to someone, especially to tell them an unpleasant truth you have been hiding.
entries.usage: Informal and mostly spoken, often as a request or promise: *Level with me*, *I'll level with you.* It signals that what follows is the frank truth, often after some evasion. It is inseparable, and the person always follows *with*.
entries.pattern: level with someone; I'll level with you
examples: Just **level with** me: is the company going to close the office or not?
I'll **level with** you, I've never actually cooked a turkey before.
The surgeon **leveled with** us and said the operation had only a fifty percent chance of working.

drill.sentence: You've been acting strange all week, so {{level with}} me: is something wrong between us?
drill.hint: speak frankly to (not *be honest with*, *be straight with* or *come clean with*)

entries.related: *be straight with someone* — same, very common; *come clean* — admit something you hid; *beat around the bush* — the opposite, avoid saying it directly.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To tell someone a secret or private information that only a few people know.
entries.usage: Informal and friendly, often with *a secret* or *the joke*: *Let me let you in on a little secret.* The person always goes between *let* and *in*. It suggests including someone in a small, trusted group.
entries.pattern: let someone in on a secret / the plan / the joke
examples: Can I **let you in on** a secret? I'm moving to Austin next month.
Nobody **let me in on** the joke, so I just smiled and nodded.
After years of begging, my aunt finally **let us in on** the secret ingredient in her chili.

drill.sentence: My sister's been hinting at big news all week, but she still won't {{let me in on}} it.
drill.hint: share the secret with me (not *fill me in on*)

entries.related: *fill someone in on* — give someone missing details, not necessarily secret; *confide in someone* — tell someone your personal secrets; *keep someone in the dark* — the opposite.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To reveal or show that you know something, especially a secret, or that you feel something.
entries.usage: Informal and mostly negative or in comparisons: *Don't let on*, *He knows more than he lets on.* It is intransitive and is usually followed by *that*, *how*, *what* or *about*, or used alone at the end of the clause. Add *to* + person for who learns it: *She never let on to her parents.*
entries.pattern: not let on (that …); know more than you let on
examples: We're throwing her a surprise party, so don't **let on** that you know.
He's a lot smarter than he **lets on**.
The owner never **let on** how close he came to selling the team.

drill.sentence: My brother was hurt by the comment, but he didn't {{let on}} until we got home.
drill.hint: reveal what he felt (not *show it*)

entries.related: *give away* — reveal by accident; *let slip* — say something secret by mistake; *keep quiet about* — not tell.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To admit honestly that you did something wrong or made a mistake.
entries.usage: Informal and common with children, partners and colleagues: *Nobody owned up.* It is intransitive, so the thing you admit follows *to*, as a noun or an *-ing* form: *own up to the mistake*, *own up to breaking it*. It sounds more personal and less formal than *admit* or *take responsibility for*.
entries.pattern: own up (to + noun / -ing)
examples: Somebody dented my car in the parking lot, and nobody **owned up**.
It took him a week to **own up to** forgetting our anniversary.
The company finally **owned up to** misleading customers about the fees.

drill.sentence: The kids swore they didn't eat the cookies, but eventually my youngest {{owned up}}.
drill.hint: admitted it was him (not *confessed* or *came clean*)

mistake.wrong: He owned up to break the vase.
mistake.right: He owned up to breaking the vase.
mistake.why: *To* here is a preposition, so it takes an *-ing* form, as in *look forward to doing*.

entries.related: *come clean* — confess something you hid; *admit (to)* — neutral and more formal; *own something* — informal, take full responsibility, as in *own your mistakes*.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To give someone, often the police or a journalist, secret information or a warning about something that is happening or about to happen.
entries.usage: Common in crime news and everyday gossip: *Police were tipped off by a neighbor.* It is very often passive, with *about* or a *that* clause for the information. A noun object can come before or after *off*, a pronoun goes in the middle (*tip them off*), and the noun is *tip-off* or simply *tip*.
entries.pattern: tip someone off (about something / that …); be tipped off
examples: Police raided the warehouse after a neighbor **tipped them off** about late-night deliveries.
Someone must have **tipped off** the press, because reporters were waiting outside the hotel.
A friend who works at the store **tipped me off** that the TVs would go on sale Friday.

drill.sentence: Thanks for {{tipping me off}} about the speed trap on Route 9; I slowed down just in time.
drill.hint: giving me a quiet warning (not *warning me* or *telling me*)

entries.related: *tip-off* — the noun; *blow the whistle* — expose wrongdoing inside an organization; *give someone a heads-up* — a friendly early warning.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To join a phone or video call quickly and informally, often at short notice.
entries.usage: Very common in American office talk, chats and emails: *Can you hop on a call?*, *Let's hop on Zoom.* It makes a call sound quick and easy, so it suits colleagues and friends more than formal clients. The call always follows *on*, the verb also works alone (*I can hop on at three*), and *hop off* means leave.
entries.pattern: hop on a call / Zoom / the line
examples: Do you have ten minutes to **hop on** a call and go over the contract?
I'll **hop on** the call from the airport, so excuse the background noise.
Our book club stopped meeting in person, so now we just **hop on** a video call once a month.

drill.sentence: The whole family is going to {{hop on}} Zoom on Sunday to sing to Grandpa for his birthday.
drill.hint: quickly join (not *jump on* or *get on*)

entries.related: *jump on a call* — same, equally informal; *join a call* — neutral; *hop off* — leave a call; *get on the phone* — start a phone conversation.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To be received with approval by an audience or group, so that people like it.
entries.usage: Used for jokes, speeches, ideas, decisions and gifts, very often in the negative: *That didn't go over well.* It is intransitive; add *with* + the audience: *go over well with voters*. British English prefers *go down well*.
entries.pattern: go over well / badly (with someone)
examples: His joke about the bride's ex didn't **go over well** with her family.
The new parking fees haven't **gone over well** with downtown business owners.
I think the speech **went over well**; people were laughing and nodding.

drill.sentence: My plan to make the whole family go vegan for Thanksgiving didn't {{go over well}} with my uncles.
drill.hint: get a positive reaction (not *land*, *sit* or *go down*)

entries.related: *go over big* — be a big success, informal; *land* — of a joke or message, work as intended; *go over like a lead balloon* — fail badly with an audience.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To talk to someone carefully, often indirectly, to find out their opinion or feelings before you decide or ask officially.
entries.usage: Used in work, politics and family situations: *sound out a colleague, investors, your parents*. It suggests tact and an informal first step before a formal request. The person usually goes in the middle (*sound him out*), but a longer noun can follow *out*, often with *about* or *on*: *sound out investors on the idea*.
entries.pattern: sound someone out (about / on something)
examples: Before I formally ask for a raise, I want to **sound out** my manager.
The school board is **sounding out** parents about a later start time for high schoolers.
Could you **sound your dad out** about lending us his truck this weekend?

drill.sentence: Before inviting everyone to Mexico for my birthday, I {{sounded out}} a few close friends to see if they'd come.
drill.hint: carefully found out the opinion of (not *felt out* or *checked with*)

entries.related: *feel someone out* — same, more American; *run something by someone* — ask for a quick opinion directly; *bounce something off someone* — share an idea to hear a reaction.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To look at someone or something carefully and form a judgment, for example about their ability, strength or character.
entries.usage: Informal and common for first meetings, opponents, rivals and new situations: *The two boxers sized each other up.* It often suggests a quick, cool, slightly suspicious assessment. A pronoun goes in the middle (*size him up*), and a noun can go before or after *up*: *size up the situation*.
entries.pattern: size someone / the situation up
examples: The two dogs circled slowly, **sizing each other up** before they started to play.
A good poker player **sizes up** the table in the first few hands.
My new manager seemed to be **sizing me up** during our first one-on-one.

drill.sentence: When I walked into the gym, the regulars looked at me as if they were {{sizing me up}}.
drill.hint: forming a quick opinion of me (not *judging* or *checking me out*)

entries.related: *check someone out* — look at someone with interest, often romantic; *weigh up* — consider carefully, more British; *take stock of* — assess a situation.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: Of facts, a story or an explanation: to make sense and seem true or consistent.
entries.usage: Mostly in the negative or in questions, especially when you suspect a lie or a mistake: *Something doesn't add up.* The subject is the story, facts or numbers, not the person. It is intransitive in this sense; separable *add something up* has the literal meaning of calculating a total.
entries.pattern: it / the story / something doesn't add up
examples: He said he was at home all night, but his story doesn't **add up**.
The official explanation for the crash doesn't **add up**, and the families want answers.
Wait, she quit her dream job to move to a town she hates? That doesn't **add up**.

drill.sentence: The landlord says he never got my rent, but I have the bank receipt. Something doesn't {{add up}}.
drill.hint: seem consistent or true (not *make sense*)

entries.related: *make sense* — neutral, more general; *check out* — be confirmed after checking; *hold water* — of an argument, be convincing.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: Of a story, claim or someone's details: to be confirmed as true or correct when someone checks it.
entries.usage: Informal and common in police work, journalism and everyday talk: *His alibi checks out.* In this sense it is intransitive, and the subject is the story, claim or reference. Do not confuse it with separable *check something out* (look at it or try it) or with checking out of a hotel.
entries.pattern: his story / alibi / references check(s) out
examples: The police called his boss, and his alibi **checked out**.
Her references all **checked out**, so we offered her the job on Friday.
I looked up the number on the letter, and it **checked out**: it really was my bank.

drill.sentence: We looked up the contractor's license number online, and everything {{checked out}}.
drill.hint: was confirmed as genuine after we looked (not *added up*)

entries.related: *add up* — make sense, even before any checking; *hold up* — remain convincing when examined; *pan out* — turn out as hoped.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: Of evidence or later events: to show that a claim, idea or prediction is true.
entries.usage: Neutral to formal, common in reports and journalism: *The figures bear this out*, *Her fears were borne out.* The subject is usually evidence or events, it is often passive (*borne out by*), and with a person as object it means confirm what they said: *The facts will bear me out.* A noun object usually follows *out*, and a pronoun goes in the middle.
entries.pattern: the evidence bears this out; be borne out by
examples: Experts warned that home prices would fall this year, and the latest figures **bear that out**.
Research has **borne out** the link between regular walking and lower blood pressure.
Scouts called him the best young pitcher in the country, and his first season **bore that out**.

drill.sentence: Mom said the new restaurant was overpriced, and our bill certainly {{bore that out}}.
drill.hint: showed it was true (not *proved*, *confirmed* or *backed up*)

entries.related: *back up* — support a claim, more informal and also used of people; *confirm* — neutral; *prove someone right* — show someone's prediction was correct.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To find or separate information, meaning or a cause carefully from something complicated or mixed up.
entries.usage: Common in analysis, therapy, interviews and journalism: *tease out the differences, the meaning, the causes*. It suggests slow, patient work, like separating knotted threads. A noun object usually follows *out*, a pronoun goes in the middle (*tease it out*), and *tease something out of someone* means get information from a reluctant person.
entries.pattern: tease out the meaning / causes / differences (from …)
examples: It's hard to **tease out** how much of the price increase comes from fuel costs and how much from demand.
A good therapist helps you **tease out** what's really bothering you.
With patience, the reporter **teased** the full story **out** of the nervous witness.

drill.sentence: Over pancakes, I slowly {{teased out}} why my teenage son had quit the basketball team.
drill.hint: carefully got the full story about (not *found out* or *figured out*)

entries.related: *draw someone out* — encourage a quiet person to talk; *disentangle* — separate mixed things, formal; *piece together* — combine bits of information.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To understand what happened by combining separate pieces of information, like the parts of a puzzle.
entries.usage: Common in stories about investigations, accidents, family history and memory: *piece together what happened, the events, a timeline*. It suggests the information came slowly and from different sources. A noun object or *what* clause usually follows *together*, and a pronoun goes in the middle: *piece it together*.
entries.pattern: piece together what happened / the events / a timeline
examples: Investigators are still trying to **piece together** what caused the crash.
From old letters and photos, she **pieced together** her grandfather's life in Italy.
I woke up with a headache and slowly **pieced together** the events of the night before.

drill.sentence: After the break-in, the neighbors shared their camera footage to help us {{piece together}} what happened.
drill.hint: build a full picture of, bit by bit (not *figure out*)

entries.related: *put two and two together* — work out the obvious truth from what you know; *reconstruct* — more formal; *figure out* — understand, in general.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To reduce a number of options or possibilities by removing the less suitable ones.
entries.usage: Very common when choosing or searching: *narrow down the list, the options, the search*. It is often followed by *to* + the remaining choices: *We've narrowed it down to two.* A pronoun goes in the middle (*narrow it down*), and a noun can go before or after *down*.
entries.pattern: narrow something down (to two / three …)
examples: We looked at fifteen apartments and finally **narrowed it down** to two.
Police have **narrowed** the list of suspects **down** to three men.
If you can **narrow down** when the bug first appeared, it'll be much easier to fix.

drill.sentence: There are so many baby names we like, but we've {{narrowed it down}} to Ava and Emma.
drill.hint: reduced the list to a few (not *cut* or *whittled*)

entries.related: *whittle down* — reduce gradually, often a list or group; *shortlist* — choose a small final group; *rule out* — remove one option.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To make plans, arrangements or details more definite and fixed.
entries.usage: Common in work emails and planning: *firm up the details, the dates, our plans*. It suggests that a rough plan already exists and now needs to be confirmed. A noun object usually follows *up*, and a pronoun goes in the middle: *firm it up*.
entries.pattern: firm up the dates / details / plans
examples: We know we're going to Maine in July, but we still need to **firm up** the dates.
Let's **firm up** the agenda by Thursday so we can send it to everyone.
The two countries met in Geneva to **firm up** the terms of the ceasefire.

drill.sentence: Let's {{firm up}} the plans for Mom's sixtieth before we start inviting people.
drill.hint: make more definite (not *finalize* or *nail down*)

entries.related: *nail down* — settle something completely and finally; *finalize* — more formal; *pencil in* — the opposite, plan something tentatively.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To secure something, such as a price, interest rate or deal, so that it cannot change in the future.
entries.usage: Common in personal finance, shopping and business: *lock in a rate, a price, your savings*. It suggests protecting yourself before conditions get worse. A noun object usually follows *in* and a pronoun goes in the middle (*lock it in*); *be locked into* a contract means be stuck in it.
entries.pattern: lock in a rate / price / deal
examples: We **locked in** a 30-year mortgage rate before rates went up again.
Book now to **lock in** this year's prices for next summer's cruise.
The new contract **locks in** his salary for the next five seasons.

drill.sentence: Electricity prices are expected to rise, so we signed a two-year plan to {{lock in}} the current rate.
drill.hint: guarantee for the future (not *secure*)

entries.related: *fix* — set a rate or price, more British in this sense; *secure* — more formal; *be locked into* — be stuck in a contract or situation.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To manage to fit someone or something into a busy schedule, often at short notice.
entries.usage: Common with doctors, hairdressers and busy people: *Can you squeeze me in today?* It shows that time is tight but you are willing to make space. The person or activity usually goes in the middle, but a noun can also follow *in*: *squeeze in a workout*.
entries.pattern: squeeze someone in; squeeze in a workout / a nap
examples: The dentist was fully booked, but she **squeezed me in** at four because of the pain.
I try to **squeeze in** a run before work, even if it's just twenty minutes.
We were only in Rome for a day, but we **squeezed in** a visit to the Pantheon.

drill.sentence: My hair appointment got canceled, but my stylist said she could {{squeeze me in}} on Saturday morning.
drill.hint: find a slot for me despite being busy (not *fit me in*)

entries.related: *fit someone in* — same, more neutral; *pencil someone in* — make a tentative appointment; *make time for* — choose to spend time on something.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To increase something, such as a price, salary, grade or priority, often by a modest amount.
entries.usage: Informal and common in speech and work chat: *bump up the price, my hours, the priority*. It often suggests a quick, small, sometimes unexpected increase. A pronoun goes in the middle (*bump it up*), and *bump someone up* means move them to a higher class or an earlier slot.
entries.pattern: bump up the price / priority; bump someone up (to …)
examples: Our landlord **bumped up** the rent by two hundred dollars a month.
The airline **bumped us up** to business class because economy was overbooked.
Since the bug affects payments, let's **bump it up** to top priority.

drill.sentence: My teacher {{bumped up}} my grade to an A after she found a mistake in how she'd added the points.
drill.hint: made higher, informally (not *raised*)

entries.related: *jack up* — raise a price sharply, more negative; *hike* — raise prices, common in news; *bump someone* — remove a passenger from an overbooked flight.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To be later than planned or scheduled, so that things start or finish late.
entries.usage: Intransitive and common with doctors' offices, meetings, flights and projects, usually in the progressive: *I'm running a little behind.* It sounds softer than *be late*, so it is a polite way to warn people. Add the amount (*running ten minutes behind*), *schedule*, or *on* + the task: *running behind on the report*.
entries.pattern: be running (ten minutes / a bit) behind (schedule / on something)
examples: Sorry, the doctor is **running** about forty minutes **behind** this afternoon.
I'm **running a little behind**, so please start the meeting without me.
The work on our kitchen is **running behind**, so we'll be cooking on a hot plate until March.

drill.sentence: Our train is {{running behind}} schedule, so we'll probably miss the connection in Chicago.
drill.hint: currently later than planned (not *falling …*)

entries.related: *run late* — same, very common; *fall behind* — gradually get later or do less than planned; *ahead of schedule* — the opposite.
